newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem talks of sharing Falklands, Britain disagrees.
newsitem.headline: Menem talks of sharing Falklands, Britain disagrees.

text.p: Argentina would be willing to share with Britain the sovereignty of the disputed Falkland Islands over which they went to war in 1982, President Carlos Menem told reporters in comments published on Monday.
But Britain, which runs the South Atlantic islands and says their sovereignty is beyond debate, quickly made it clear it opposes shared rule.

"Our position is clear. We cannot discuss the sovereignty of the islands, or surrender them or share them," said Defence Minister Michael Portillo, passing through Argentina's neighbour Chile before making a visit to the islands.

About 1,000 soldiers, mostly Argentine, died in the 10-week war when Britain sent a task force and ousted troops trying to enforce Argentine sovereignty. Argentina lost the war but maintains its claim.

Diplomatic ties have resumed and Menem has promoted close trade and diplomatic links with Britain while insisting Argentina will win back the islands. He said in his native La Rioja province on Sunday that he hoped to see the Argentine flag flying there "alone or with other flags" by 2000.
Asked if that meant shared rule of the islands Argentina calls the Malvinas, he replied: "To have the Argentine flag flying in the islands for example with the English flag would be a step forward."

However the British embassy in Buenos Aires said there was no change in London's position of "supporting the islanders' right to self-determination -- and they have made it clear they have no wish to change their present status."

Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella has attracted criticism for a "charm offensive" that has included sending the islanders Christmas cards with photos of his family. But he recently acknowledged: "I haven't had any results for six years."
He was on vacation on Monday but ministry officials said Menem's words "cannot be questioned, this is an order."
Menem portrayed shared rule as a "change with the times" and said: "We have never had such good relations with England as we do now. So our chances of recovering the islands are better."
But for the opposition, it was an admission of failure.

Radical Party deputy Marcelo Stubrin, deputy head of the lower house of Congress' Foreign Affairs Committee, told local news agency DyN: "We've said again and again the seduction strategy was not working and now the government admits it."
And Juan Pablo Cafiero, deputy for the centre-left Frepaso coalition, told DyN that Menem's new strategy "is not going to be believed in London or here."
